name: Urban and Rural Areas and Population Density

scenes.animation: Zippy hosts a birthday party in a small room: first five friends dance comfortably, then the doorbell rings and thirty more squeeze in until Zippy is pressed flat against the wall like a sticker.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Neo, help! Same room, more people, and suddenly I can't breathe!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Congratulations, Zippy. You have just discovered population density.

scenes.animation: A scroll unrolls with sketches of Harappan Dholavira, Kalibangan and Rakhigarhi, then Vijayanagara, Varanasi and Ujjain, each glowing on a map of India. The scroll then morphs into a modern skyline.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: India has a rich urban legacy. Think of Harappan cities like Dholavira, Kalibangan and Rakhigarhi, and historic ones like Vijayanagara, Varanasi and Ujjain.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Many of these cities are still flourishing today.

scenes.animation: Split screen. Left: a city with dense buildings, offices, a bus stand and a municipal office labelled 'Elected local body'. Right: a village with fields, a close-knit chaupal and a sign 'Gram Panchayat'. Labels list features on each side.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Urban areas have many people, many kinds of businesses and jobs, government institutions, and big transport and communication systems. Elected local bodies look after them.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Rural areas are villages with fewer people, close-knit communities, more farm-based work, and gram panchayats.

scenes.animation: Three flags pop up with counters: Denmark '220', Japan '50,000', India '5,000', each labelled 'people needed to count as urban'. Zippy's eyes spin between the numbers.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So how many people make a place a town?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It depends on the country! In Denmark, a place becomes urban above 220 people. In Japan, 50,000. In India, 5,000.

scenes.animation: The formula builds on a blackboard: 'Population density = total population of a region / area in sq km'. Then two satellite views from Haryana slide in side by side: village Asadpur Khera with green and brown fields, and Gurugram with grey built-up blocks. Dots representing people pack densely into Gurugram.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Population density is the number of people living per square kilometre. Divide the total population of a region by its area.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Look at these satellite views from Haryana. The village has open fields. Gurugram is packed with buildings, so its density is much higher.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two of the world's most populous cities are in India: Kolkata and New Delhi.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: always write the unit, people per square kilometre, when you give a density answer.

scenes.animation: The party room clears out as three recap points appear on the wall like party banners.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: India has an urban legacy from Harappan cities to Varanasi and Ujjain. Two: urban areas have elected local bodies, while villages have gram panchayats, and India counts a place as urban above 5,000 people. Three: population density is people per square kilometre.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Next party, I am booking a stadium.

name: How Cities Become Centres of Economic Activities

scenes.animation: A tiny village with one tea stall. Time-lapse: a road appears, then a small factory, then a bank, a hotel, a bus stand, until high-rises and a metro line surround the original tea stall, now a busy chai cafe.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Whoa! That tea stall grew a whole city around it!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That is urbanisation. Villages slowly become towns, and towns become cities.

scenes.animation: A map shows old cities growing beside rivers, at crossroads of trade routes, and near farmland and mines. A pie chart morphs from '17% urban (1951)' to 'about 40% urban (2025)' for India, and a globe label reads '55% now, 68% by 2050'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Places grew into cities because they were near rivers, on trade routes, or close to farm produce and raw materials.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Today, 55 per cent of the world lives in cities, and the United Nations expects 68 per cent by 2050.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In India, the urban population rose from 17 per cent in 1951 to around 40 per cent in 2025.

scenes.animation: A flowchart of Fig. 7.6 builds step by step: 'Rural origins: farm work' then 'Early urbanisation: small industries, transport, services' then 'Small towns and trading centres' then 'People arrive, population grows' then 'New infrastructure and many kinds of jobs' then 'Metropolitan area'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It starts with farm work. Then small industries, transport and services appear. Small towns and trading centres emerge.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: People arrive for jobs. Factories, banks, hotels and stadiums are built. Finally, cities expand into metropolitan areas.

scenes.animation: A map of Jharkhand zooms into the Chota Nagpur Plateau: the village Sakchi sits beside glowing iron ore. A steel plant rises, tree-lined streets and gardens are drawn in, and the signboard changes from 'Sakchi' to 'Jamshedpur, 1919'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Sakchi was a small village near rich iron ore deposits. It was chosen as the site of Asia's first steel plant.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Tata family planned a township with wide, tree-lined streets and gardens. Sakchi was renamed Jamshedpur in 1919. Today it is Jharkhand's largest industrial city.

scenes.animation: A map of India highlights Mumbai on the Arabian Sea and Kolkata near the eastern coast with ship icons. In Mumbai, a 'BSE 1875' building appears, then a film reel from the 1910s, then the Bandra Worli Sea Link.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So every city needs iron ore?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No! Location matters too. Mumbai on the Arabian Sea and Kolkata near the eastern coast became port cities for trade.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: After the Bombay Stock Exchange was set up in 1875, Mumbai became India's financial capital. Its film industry began in the 1910s.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: urbanisation means a population shift from rural to urban areas. Learn that definition exactly.

scenes.animation: The Jamshedpur and Mumbai scenes shrink into postcards; three recap points appear beside them.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: cities grew near rivers, trade routes and raw materials. Two: India's urban population rose from 17 per cent in 1951 to around 40 per cent in 2025. Three: Jamshedpur grew from iron ore, while Mumbai grew as a port and financial capital.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Next stop, my tea stall's metro line!

name: Specialised Cities and Cities as Cultural Hubs

scenes.animation: Zippy runs a quiz show with buzzers. On screen: a brass pot, a wooden toy, a silk saree and a laptop. Contestants must match each to a city on a map of India.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Quiz time! Brass pot, wooden toy, silk saree, laptop. Which city makes what?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Easy. Many Indian cities are famous for one special thing. Let's put them on the map.

scenes.animation: A map of India fills pin by pin: Bengaluru and Hyderabad with laptop icons; Moradabad with brass; Ludhiana and Tirupur with textiles; Jaipur with gems and handicrafts; Channapatna with wooden toys; Kanchipuram with silk sarees.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Bengaluru, the Silicon Valley of India, grew as an IT hub with software firms, start-ups and colleges working closely together. Hyderabad is a major tech centre too.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Moradabad is known for brass, Ludhiana and Tirupur for textiles, Jaipur for handicrafts and gem jewellery, Channapatna for wooden toys, and Kanchipuram for silk sarees.

scenes.animation: The Taj Mahal glows in Agra with a visitor counter reading '70-80 lakh a year'. Pilgrims walk towards Amritsar and Varanasi, where flower sellers, tea stalls, rickshaws and saree shops light up.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Some cities thrive on history and faith. Agra, home to the Taj Mahal, gets 70 to 80 lakh visitors every year.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Pilgrims visit Amritsar and Varanasi. This supports transport, hotels, food vendors and handicrafts.

scenes.animation: A timeline of Delhi builds: 'Iron Age', 'Rajputs, Turks, Mughals: forts, roads, markets', 'British: new capital, railways, electricity', 'After 1947: capital of the Republic'. Then a map of NCR expands to include NOIDA, Ghaziabad and Gurugram, with metro lines drawn in.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Delhi has been a centre of culture, trade and administration since the Iron Age. After Independence, New Delhi became the capital of the Republic.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: As it grew crowded, the National Capital Region was created, including NOIDA and Ghaziabad. Since the 1990s, Gurugram has become a major IT and BPO hub.

scenes.animation: A Mumbai mill worker bites into a vada pav; labels float over it: 'Maharashtrian potato vada' and 'pav: Portuguese'. Then Kolkata's Durga Puja pandals light up with a UNESCO badge '2021', beside libraries, museums and stadiums.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Do cities only make money?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No, they mix cultures too. Mumbai's vada pav combines a Maharashtrian potato vada with Portuguese-style pav. It became popular with textile mill workers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Kolkata's Durga Puja was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2021.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: in map work, practise locating these specialised cities on an outline map of India.

scenes.animation: The quiz board flips to show three recap points as the final answers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: many cities specialise, like Bengaluru in IT and Moradabad in brass. Two: tourism and pilgrimage support cities like Agra, Amritsar and Varanasi. Three: cities are cultural hubs, from vada pav to Kolkata's Durga Puja.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I'm taking a vada pav as my prize.

scenes.animation: Zippy rides an auto-rickshaw through a city: a traffic jam, a hazy sky, an overflowing garbage heap and a flooded underpass flash past. The auto stalls, and Zippy coughs a small grey cloud.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Cities are exciting, but why is everything jammed, smoky and flooded?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because too many people and too little planning put pressure on resources.

scenes.animation: A collage of Fig. 7.18 assembles tile by tile: poor air quality, water scarcity, traffic jams, reduced green spaces, waste generation, flooding during monsoons, urban slums. A thermometer rises over a grey block labelled 'Heat island'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: More people need more food, water, energy and housing. Roads get crowded, unplanned colonies grow, and waste piles up.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Concrete creates heat islands, raising temperatures. Crime can also be higher because of density and inequality.

scenes.animation: An AQI meter over NCR swings past '400' into deep red while a green zone at '50' is marked 'safe limit'. Masked children wait at a bus stop.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The National Capital Region often records Air Quality Index levels over 400. The safe limit is 50.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: That's eight times over the safe limit!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes, and it poses serious health risks to residents.

scenes.animation: Beside a railway track, crowded shacks with little water or drainage. Residents head out as a vegetable vendor, domestic helper, construction worker and plumber. A new building rises with a board 'Pradhan Mantri Aawaas Yojana'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Slums are overcrowded settlements with poor housing, water and sanitation. They grow near railway tracks and industrial areas, because there is not enough affordable housing.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Slum dwellers support the city by selling vegetables, doing domestic help, construction and plumbing. The Pradhan Mantri Aawaas Yojana provides affordable housing for economically weaker households.

scenes.animation: A map of Bengaluru is dotted with about 1,000 blue lakes that fade until about 200 remain; Bellandur and Varthur froth with foam and a small flame. Then volunteers desilt, repair bunds, plant native plants and release fish, and Yelahanka Lake turns clear blue.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Bengaluru once had around 1,000 lakes. Rapid urbanisation reduced them to about 200, and many were polluted. Bellandur and Varthur lakes even caught fire!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now nonprofits, Resident Welfare Associations and communities are reviving lakes by desilting, repairing bunds and planting native species.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: when asked about urban challenges, give a problem and a solution, like Bengaluru's lake revival.

scenes.animation: Clear blue sky returns over the city as three recap points appear on a billboard.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: crowded cities face traffic, pollution, waste, heat islands and floods. Two: slums grow when affordable housing is short, yet slum dwellers keep cities running. Three: collective action, like reviving Bengaluru's lakes, can fix problems.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Community power beats traffic jams!

scenes.animation: Zippy plays a city-building game on a tablet, dropping a factory next to a school and a highway through a park. Alarms blare and pixel citizens wave angry signs.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: My game city is a disaster! Everyone is angry!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That is why real cities need urban planners. Let's learn from the best.

scenes.animation: An urban planner walk-on unrolls a blueprint with questions popping up: 'How many people?', 'What jobs?', 'What transport?', 'Where do homes, parks, schools and hospitals go?', 'Safe streets, fire and police stations?'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Planners ask many questions. How many people live here? What jobs do they do? How will they travel?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Where should homes, parks, schools and hospitals go? And how do we keep streets safe for walkers and cyclists?

scenes.animation: A 1727 parchment unrolls: a grid of rectangular blocks labelled 'chowkris', wide streets, nine public squares, and a wall with seven gates built step by step. The buildings turn pink sandstone, and a stepwell fills with water.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1727, Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II asked Vidyadhar Bhattacharya to design Jaipur. He used vastu shastra and shilpa shastra.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The city had a grid of blocks called chowkris, wide streets and nine public squares. A 20-foot wall with seven gates kept it safe.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Buildings used pink sandstone, which is why Jaipur is called the Pink City.

scenes.animation: A globe zooms to Singapore: an overcrowded 1960s port transforms into green high-rises with vertical gardens. Labels appear: 'Over 8,000 people per sq km', 'Concept Plan: 40 years ahead', 'Master Plan: updated every 5 years'. An MRT train and park connectors link the city.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: What about a modern example?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Singapore has over 8,000 people per square kilometre, yet a high quality of life. Its Concept Plan looks up to 40 years ahead, and its Master Plan is updated every 5 years.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It mixes homes, offices and parks nearby, links rail, buses and cycle paths, and grows vertical gardens on buildings.

scenes.animation: Back in India: the Sabarmati Riverfront in Ahmedabad with promenades and the Atal Bridge, then Gangtok's M.G. Road, a clean pedestrian-only shopping street. An 'Exam Tip' card flips beside Jaipur's grid.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: India has fine examples too. Ahmedabad's Sabarmati Riverfront has parks, promenades and the Atal Bridge. Gangtok's M.G. Road is a clean, pedestrian-only hub.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: remember Jaipur's chief planner, Vidyadhar Bhattacharya, and the year 1727.

scenes.animation: Zippy's game city rebuilds itself neatly with parks and metro lines as three recap points appear.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: urban planners decide where people live, work, travel and play. Two: Jaipur, planned in 1727, used grids, squares and pink sandstone. Three: Singapore plans ahead and updates often, while India has spaces like the Sabarmati Riverfront.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: My city just got a garden on every wall!
